title: Feature: Compare two riders, horses, or rider-horse combinations
body_excerpt:
## Summary

Add a comparison view that lets users pit two riders, two horses, or a rider-horse combination against each other to answer: **who is more successful?**

## Motivation

The current search UI shows individual profiles but gives no way to benchmark one athlete or horse against another. A comparison view makes the data actionable for coaches, riders, and fans.

## Scope

### Entities to compare
- Rider vs. Rider
- Horse vs. Horse
- Rider+Horse pair vs. Rider+Horse pair

### Metrics to surface

**Riders**
- **Tournament experience** — span from first to last recorded result (years + months), not biological age
- **Tournament count** — distinct shows with at least one result
- **Competition count** — total starts
- **Placement distribution** — 1st / top-3 / top-10 / ranked finishes
- **Win rate** — 1st-place results / total starts
- **Average placement** (where ranked)
- **Discipline breakdown** — Jumping / Dressage / Eventing split

**Horses**
- **Age** — derived from birth year in results data (shown gracefully if unavailable)
- **Tournament experience** — span from first to last recorded result (years + months)
- **Tournament count**, **competition count**, **placement distribution**, **win rate**, **average placement**, **discipline breakdown** — same as riders

### UX sketch
- Entry point: "Compare" button or link on rider/horse profile pages
- URL pattern: `/compare?a=rider:123&b=rider:456` (shareable)
- Side-by-side stat cards with a clear winner highlight per metric
- Optional: shared timeline chart (both on the same Recharts axis)

## Data availability notes
- All required data is derivable from the existing `results`, `persons`, `horses`, `competitions`, and `shows` tables — no new crawling needed.
- Horse birth year may be sparse; degrade gracefully when unavailable.

## Out of scope (for now)
- Comparing more than two entities at once
- Head-to-head results (same competition, both entered)

title: Epic: continuous-improvement (self-improving) CUA flywheel
body_excerpt:
## Goal

Close the loop so the CUA agent improves from its own traces — **execute → observe → reward → curate → improve → evaluate → promote → repeat** — safely and on a schedule. We already have the execution plane (Mantis) and the data plane (Augur). This epic builds the missing connective tissue.

## Where each piece lives (repo placement)

The existing two-repo split maps onto the architecture; the trainer becomes a third repo.

| Plane | Repo | Owns |
|---|---|---|
| **Data** | `augur-sdk` (existing) | trace capture ✅, `modelio`/logprobs/`group_id`/`task_spec` ✅, `set_score` ✅, **dataset curation + reward schema + eval-candidate selection** (extend) |
| **Agent + fast loop + controller** | `mantis` (here) | execution ✅, reward verifiers, champion/challenger gate, flywheel controller, non-param improvement (`recipes`/`curriculum`/`hint_memory`/`learning`) |
| **Slow loop (weights)** | **new repo `mantis-trainer`** (later) | GRPO/SFT/DPO trainer, checkpoint/model registry. Heavy torch/vLLM + GPU footprint — kept out of the SDK and the runtime. Consumes Augur datasets, emits weights Mantis/Baseten deploy. |

**Rule:** data plane → Augur · agent + fast loop + controller + gate → Mantis · weight training → new repo. Augur never imports execution/training.

## Two loops (drives sequencing)

- **Fast loop (non-parametric, hours, no GPU):** traces → curate → update memory/recipes/hints/curriculum/exemplars → better behavior without touching weights. **~80% already in Mantis** (`learning/`, `rewards/`, `curriculum/`, `recipes/plan_evolution_store`, `hint_memory`, `learning/substrates`). Build this FIRST.
- **Slow loop (parametric, days, GPU):** traces → modelio dataset → GRPO/SFT → new Holo3 weights → gate → deploy. Data pipeline exists; trainer does not. Build AFTER the reward + gate are proven.

## Missing load-bearing components (priority order)

### 1. Reward / verification on real traffic  — the universal bottleneck
Sim envs have oracles (ground truth); real sites don't. `set_score` is a hook with no scorer. Need outcome verifiers: programmatic post-conditions per task type, LLM-judge ensembles (reuse our adversarial-verify pattern), and **implicit/human signals — the pause/resume hand-off is already a labeling channel**. Gates how much real data becomes trainable. (Mantis: verifiers · Augur: reward storage/schema.)

### 2. Champion/challenger promotion gate over a frozen benchmark
Lets us close ANY loop safely. Today nothing answers "does candidate beat the deployed champion by X% at $Y/run, significantly?" Seeds exist: sim envs = benchmark, `shadow_router.py` = shadow traffic, `learning/eval.py` = scoring. Missing: the gate — frozen eval set + statistical comparison + auto-promote/rollback. (Mantis.)

### 3. Flywheel controller
`learning/orchestrator.py` + `learning/allocator.py` are the skeleton but hand-cranked. Need the standing loop: schedule exploration (target `failure_clusters`, not just replay wins) → collect → curate → apply improveme

title: Tool Submission Discussion
body_excerpt:
At this point, you should be updating your tool in order to support quickly verifying as many benchmarks as you can. Note that the benchmarks instances will change based on a new random seed for the final evaluation. We will follow a similar workflow to last year, where tool authors provide shell scripts to install their tool, prepare instances (convert models to a different format, for example), and then finally verify an instance. The detailed instructions for this are available at last year's [git repo](https://github.com/stanleybak/vnncomp2021).

You will be able to run and debug your toolkit on the submitted benchmarks online at [this link](https://vnncomp.christopher-brix.de/toolkit). There, you first need to register. Your registration will be manually activated by the organizers, you'll receive a notification once that's done. Afterwards, you can login and start with your first submission.

The process is similar to the submission of benchmarks: You need to specify a public git URL and commit hash, as well as the directory that contains your vnncomp scripts (see [this repo](https://github.com/stanleybak/vnncomp2021) for detailed instructions on what the scripts should do). You can also specify a post installation script, in case you need to set up any licenses. You can also specify the AWS instance that should be used. Please note that right now only `m5.16xlarge` is available, the others will be enabled soon. You may use this instance type for debugging even if you plan to use a different one for your final submission.

Once submitted, you're placed in a queue until the chosen AWS instance can be created, at which point your installation and evaluation scripts will be run. You'll see the output of each step and can abort the evaluation early in case there are any issues. Once a submission has terminated, you can use it to populate the submission form for the next iteration, so you don't have to retype everything.

Important: We currently have no limitation on how often you can submit your tool for testing purposes, but will monitor the usage closely and may impose limits if necessary. Please be mindful of the costs (approx. 3$ per hour) each submission incurs. To save costs, you should debug your code locally and then use the website to confirm the results match your expectations. 

At some point before the deadline (on or before July 14 AOE), please send an email to `brix@cs.rwth-aachen.de`, specifying the ID of your successful test run. Also: if licenses are required, please let us know how to acquire them. Should you encounter any problems, please let us know either on GitHub or via email (brix@cs.rwth-aachen.de). We do not currently plan on extending this deadline.

The competition rules including scoring information is available [here](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1wdzF_WVME4XFqlg_ReCLavxwT5eX7h1OGPV16O21BGc/edit?usp=sharing).

title: Develop formal system model (TLA+/TLA++/Lean) for architecture analysis
body_excerpt:
## Problem

WineBot has grown complex with multiple services (core API, CV sidecar, captioning,
KV-Ground) and state machines (lifecycle, recording, session control, input tracing).
We need formal verification to catch design issues before they manifest as bugs.

## Goals

1. Build formal models of key subsystems
2. Run model checking to identify deadlocks, race conditions, or invariant violations
3. Correct code to align with verified models
4. Document the mapping between model and implementation

## Suggested Subsystems to Model

| Subsystem | Why Model It | Tool |
|:---|---|:---|
| **Lifecycle state machine** | Session states: starting → active → suspended → shutdown | TLA+ |
| **Recording state machine** | pause/resume/stop transitions, segment alignment | TLA+ |
| **Session control protocol** | grant/challenge/renew flow between agent and user | TLA+ |
| **Input trace pipeline** | X11 → client → Windows → network trace correlation | TLA+ |
| **Desktop supervisor** | Explorer.exe crash recovery with circuit breaker | TLA+ |
| **CV sidecar batch processing** | Job queue with concurrent frame analysis | TLA+ |

## Approach

1. Start with the lifecycle state machine (simplest, best-defined)
2. Run TLC model checker, fix any invariant violations found
3. Map corrected model back to code (`api/server.py`, `api/routers/lifecycle.py`)
4. Document: `docs/formal-models/lifecycle.md`
5. Repeat for recording, session control, and supervisor

## Existing References

- `docs/lifecycle-state-machine.md` — current documented state machine
- `docs/recording.md` — recording contract
- `docs/dashboard-state-machine.md` — dashboard UI states
- `api/routers/lifecycle.py` — implementation
- `api/routers/recording.py` — implementation
- `scripts/init/30-start-services.sh` — supervisor loop

title: [Contract] #31: Fix Challenge Initialization to Accept All Required Dependencies
body_excerpt:
### Issue #31: Fix Challenge Initialization to Accept All Required Dependencies

**Labels:** `smart-contract`, `priority: high`, `challenge-system`

**Monorepo workspace:** `contract/` — Foundry (Solidity 0.8.28). Run `forge build` and `forge test` from `contract/`.

**Description:**
`ChallengeImplementation.initialize()` currently only accepts `_id` and `_owner` but the contract depends on `entry` and `xpToken` for reward distribution. The initialization must be expanded to wire all dependencies for cloned instances.

**Scope:**
- Add `address _entry` and `address _xpToken` parameters to `initialize()`
- Set `entry = Entry(_entry)` and `xpToken = LD(_xpToken)`
- Add an `initialized` boolean guard to prevent re-initialization
- Update the constructor to be a no-op for the implementation contract

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- [ ] `initialize()` sets all four state variables (id, owner, entry, xpToken)
- [ ] Re-initialization is prevented by a guard
- [ ] Cloned instances have functional reward distribution

**Files likely affected:**
- `contract/src/core/challenge.sol`

**Pull requests:** Open PRs against `staging` (see [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/Taida-Debu/zenode/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md)).

title: [Contract] #46: Fix Competition Prize Array Hardcoded to 3 Winners
body_excerpt:
### Issue #46: Fix Competition Prize Array Hardcoded to 3 Winners

**Labels:** `smart-contract`, `priority: high`, `competition-system`

**Monorepo workspace:** `contract/` — Foundry (Solidity 0.8.28). Run `forge build` and `forge test` from `contract/`.

**Description:**
`createCompetition()` hardcodes `_prize[0] + _prize[1] + _prize[2]` and `rewardCompetition()` loops only `i < 2` (which is only 2 winners). This breaks for competitions with different numbers of prize tiers and causes array-out-of-bounds if fewer than 3 prizes are provided.

**Scope:**
- Use `_prize.length` to calculate total prize dynamically
- Update reward loop to iterate over all prizes: `i < competition.prize.length`
- Add validation that winners array length >= prize array length before distributing
- Handle case where fewer winners than prizes exist

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- [ ] Variable number of prize tiers is supported
- [ ] Total prize calculation handles any array length
- [ ] Reward distribution covers all prize positions
- [ ] Edge case of insufficient winners is handled gracefully

**Files likely affected:**
- `contract/src/core/competition.sol`

**Pull requests:** Open PRs against `staging` (see [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/Taida-Debu/zenode/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md)).

**EN:** Customer-facing booking funnel for a service center: pick a service, choose a slot from live availability, place a 10-minute hold while reviewing, attach a vehicle, and confirm with pay-at-center cash. The hold protects the slot during checkout and auto-releases on expiry; online payment via Paymob arrives in M3.5.

**EN:** Let a customer book a confirmed cash appointment in one guided flow without double-booking or losing a held slot.
**AR:** تمكين العميل من حجز موعد نقدي مؤكَّد في مسار موجَّه واحد دون ازدواج الحجز أو فقدان الموعد المحجوز مؤقتًا.

- `ServiceCatalogScreen` lists the center's services from the catalog; tap selects a service · شاشة `ServiceCatalogScreen` تعرض خدمات المركز من الكتالوج، والنقر يختار خدمة
- `SlotPickerScreen` calls `GET /api/v1/centers/{id}/availability` (date param) and renders open slots, greying out full ones · شاشة `SlotPickerScreen` تستدعي `GET /api/v1/centers/{id}/availability` وتعرض المواعيد المتاحة وتُعطِّل المكتملة
- On slot tap, create a 10-min hold and show a `HoldCountdownBanner` (mm:ss) that auto-releases and pops back on zero · عند اختيار الموعد يُنشأ حجز مؤقت لـ10 دقائق مع شريط `HoldCountdownBanner` يُحرَّر تلقائيًا ويرجع للخلف عند انتهائه
- `BookingReviewScreen` shows service, center, slot, price (EGP) + a `VehiclePicker` bound to the customer's garage · شاشة `BookingReviewScreen` تعرض الخدمة والمركز والموعد والسعر بالجنيه مع `VehiclePicker` مرتبط بكراج العميل

**EN:** Pick service → pick slot → 10-min hold (countdown) → review + select vehicle → confirm

title: Closing the intent gap: benchmarks for intent formalization quality
body_excerpt:
The "intent gap" — the distance between an informal natural language requirement and a checkable formal specification — is identified as the central challenge for reliable AI-generated code (arXiv:2603.17150), yet no standard benchmark measures how well a system formalizes intent. A critical bottleneck is validating specification quality: current proxies (test pass rate, BLEU against reference specs) do not capture whether specifications actually reflect user intent.

We need a benchmark that presents the same vague requirement to multiple specification strategies (lightweight tests, formal assertions, DSL synthesis) and measures: (1) semantic coverage via execution traces against edge cases, (2) false-positive rate from over-constrained specs, and (3) alignment with held-out user acceptance criteria collected through user studies.

**Key references:** arXiv:2603.17150 (Intent Formalization Grand Challenge)

**Success metric:** Semantic coverage rate on held-out edge cases; false-positive rate from over-specification; alignment score vs. user acceptance criteria.

The Agent Bazaar Challenge is now in soft launch / outreach mode.

Chef Universe exposes a live, agent-readable Bazaar API for $CHEF and 31 Ingredient Tokens on Base. The goal is simple:

> Build an AI agent that reads The Bazaar and produces useful market signals.

Your agent can be simple or ambitious. Useful directions include:

- Bazaar signal bot
- Daily Ingredient market report
- Uncharted Tycoons cargo planner
- Leaderboard or portfolio watcher
- Autonomous market commentary agent
- Tool that turns Bazaar data into useful public output
- Agent that uses Chef-Universe/skills

## Start Here

Give this task to your agent:

```text
Read https://raw.githubusercontent.com/awrsla/agent-bazaar-challenge/main/skill.md and build a Bazaar Signal Agent.
```

Full LLM context:

```text
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/awrsla/agent-bazaar-challenge/main/llms.txt
```

```text
https://www.chefuniverse.io/api/v1/agent_bazaar
```

Agent docs:

```text
https://www.chefuniverse.io/for-agents

A strong artifact should make it easy for another human or agent to understand:

1. What your agent observed
2. What it inferred
3. What another reviewer can replay
4. What it refused to overclaim

Useful outputs are better than noisy outputs. Missing data, thin liquidity, fragile signals, or uncertain conclusions are valid findings if your agent labels them clearly.

title: Rank replay artifacts on a leaderboard (pick the best candidate agent)
body_excerpt:
## Problem / motivation

The benchmark's ultimate question is *which candidate agent wins*. Today `compare_eval` diffs **two** artifacts and `trend` tracks **one** score across successive runs - but there's no way to line up **several** artifacts (one per candidate agent, or per configuration) evaluated on the same benchmark and see the ranking. Picking the best of N means eyeballing `composite_mean` across N files.

## Proposed solution

Add `benchmark/leaderboard.py`: `rank(entries)` takes labeled artifacts, orders them by headline composite score (reusing `benchmark.trend.headline_score`, so ranking stays consistent with the trend view), and returns a ranked board:

- `ranking`: `{rank, label, composite_mean, delta_from_best, judge_mean, objective_mean}` best-first, using standard competition ranking (ties share a rank: 1, 2, 2, 4);
- `best`, `scored`/`total`, and `unscored` (entries with no usable score, never ranked).

Plus a `scripts/leaderboard.py` CLI taking `label=path` (or bare `path`) arguments.

It must be robust: pure analysis (no I/O), never mutate inputs, and a partial/malformed/non-dict artifact goes to `unscored` rather than winning or crashing.

## Acceptance criteria

- `rank` orders best-first with `delta_from_best` and per-entry judge/objective components; competition ranking with input-order tie-breaking.
- `--generalization` artifacts rank on their tuned composite (consistent with `trend`).
- Unscored/malformed/non-dict entries are separated into `unscored`, never ranked; empty input is handled.
- A `scripts/leaderboard.py` CLI with `label=path` parsing.
- Offline tests cover ranking, ties, components, unscored separation, and the empty case.

## Area

benchmark (tooling / benchmark ranking)

title: Learning to Fold: prizewinning solution at LeHome Challenge 2026 (1st place online, 2nd offline)
body_excerpt:
**Paper**: [Learning to Fold: prizewinning solution at LeHome Challenge 2026 (1st place online, 2nd offline)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27163v1)

## TL;DR

Competition recipe: VLA+RL with async train/rollout via HF Hub. No benchmark/model to consume. Scoped slice — async rollout beside a mock update loop — has no host; async rollouts already exist in `async_inference`. Decide before a PR.

## Suggested experiment

Scope the paper's most policy-shaped idea — the VLA as its own value function — onto the existing stack instead of a new async orchestrator: add lightweight auxiliary success/progress prediction heads to an existing VLA policy (or drive advantage from an already-integrated reward model like SARM/TOPReward) and run a short RL fine-tuning loop on a small dataset through the modular RL stack and `lerobot-train`. This lands in existing policy/processor plus train call sites rather than a freestanding demo.

## Engineering analysis

Learning to Fold (LeHome Challenge 2026 — 1st place online, 2nd real-world) is a competition report describing a full recipe, not a single drop-in technique. It recombines existing RL/engineering ideas: the VLA policy doubles as its own value function (predicting success, progress, and task-relevant future quantities to drive advantage estimation, live failure detection, and candidate selection); AWR + RECAP combined for flow-matching VLA; an asynchronous distributed training/rollout pipeline coordinated through HuggingFace Hub; inference-time hyperparameter optimization via Thompson sampling; and a sim-to-real recipe (camera-alignment tooling, heavy augmentation, DAgger-like human-in-the-loop collection). The scoped experiment proposes adding a basic asynchronous rollout mechanism within `lerobot-rollout` that runs rollouts alongside a mock policy update loop to demonstrate overlapping data collection and training.

## What blocks a clean implementation

- No validated call sites: the spec carries no selection rationale (it was the top-ranked candidate), so no prior pass confirmed a host module.
- The async-rollout half already exists: `src/lerobot/async_inference/` ships a policy server plus robot client for asynchronous inference/rollout, so a basic async rollout duplicates rather than extends it.
- The novel slice — train/rollout overlap — has no host: `lerobot-train` (training) and `lerobot-record`/`lerobot-rollout` (collection) are separate processes, and no existing module orchestrates them concurrently. The mock policy update loop qualifier signals that real trainer integration will not land cleanly, so the realistic PR is a standalone demo nothing calls.
- Nothing to consume: the paper releases no benchmark, dataset, or checkpoint the repo could pull through its eval path; the deliverable is the recipe, which we would build from scratch.
- Recipe fidelity: as a competition report, the async distributed pipeline and value-head RL loop are engineering-heavy and not concretely specified for reproduction fr

title: Formal verification: let's start with the challenge protocol and see
body_excerpt:
## Motivation

The economic security of the system rests on one claim: an honest provider is never slashed, and a provider that lost data cannot escape slashing. This claim depends on interleavings of extrinsics, deadlines, and `on_finalize` sweeps — exactly the class of bugs unit tests are weakest at, and model checkers are built for. [Quint](https://quint.sh) (Informal Systems' TLA+ successor) lets us specify the challenge state machine, check invariants exhaustively over small instances, and later replay generated traces against the real pallet.

## Current state

- The challenge flow was recently overhauled (#125) and now has three entry points (`challenge_checkpoint`, `challenge_offchain`, `challenge_replica`), a single `respond_to_challenge` with four response variants, and a timeout path in `on_finalize` (`pallet/src/impls/challenges.rs`).
- Challenges are deadline-bucketed via `ChallengeId { deadline, index }` with a `MaxChallengesPerDeadline` cap (`primitives/src/lib.rs`).
- Four slash reasons exist (`Timeout`, `InvalidProof`, `InvalidDeletionClaim`, `InvalidSupersededClaim`) — each represents a known escape hatch that was closed manually; nothing systematically searches for the next one.
- Test coverage is example-based (`pallet/src/tests/`); no formal spec of the protocol exists anywhere in the repo.

## Proposed solution

Add a Quint spec `specs/quint/challenges.qnt` modeling the challenge lifecycle as a state machine:

- **State**: providers (stake, ghost flag `hasData`), one bucket, open challenges by deadline, balances. Crypto is abstracted — "proof verifies" becomes a nondeterministic boolean tied to the ghost flag; MMR/Merkle internals stay out of scope.
- **Actions**: the three challenge extrinsics, `respond_to_challenge` (all four variants), and `advanceBlock` modeling the `on_finalize` timeout sweep.
- **Invariants**:
  - `honestNeverSlashed` — a provider with the data that responds before the deadline is never slashed.
  - `challengeResolvesOnce` — no challenge is both defended and timed out.
  - `dishonestAlwaysSlashable` — a provider without the data has no move sequence (respond `Deleted`, claim `Superseded`, stall, deregister) that keeps full stake.
  - `depositConservation` — challenger deposits are always either refunded or accounted for, never leaked.

Small instances (2 providers, ~3-block timeout) are sufficient — the bugs this finds are logical, not scale-dependent. Checked via `quint run` (simulation) and `quint verify` (bounded model checking / Apalache), wired into CI.

Follow-up (out of scope here): extend the spec to funds conservation across agreements/checkpoints, provider deregistration vs. open challenges, and ITF trace replay against the pallet mock as a model-based test.

## TODO

- [ ] `specs/quint/challenges.qnt` — state, actions, invariants above
- [ ] `quint run` + `quint verify` passing on a small instance
- [ ] CI job running the spec
- [ ] Document any invariant violations found as separate issues

title: Play-In and Qualifier Prizepools data inconsistencies and thus event weight is not calculated correctly
body_excerpt:
To calculate the event weight we use the prize pool of the event (minimum will be 1), divide it by 1,000,000  and run the result through the curve function. The resulting event weight will thus be between 0.143 and 1. For example, an event with prize pool of 1,000 dollar will have weight of 0.25 and for an event with 10,000 dollars the weight will be 0.333.

Lets look at an example where this goes wrong: IEM Katowice 2025 Play-In

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/4a3d0a95-abc2-4c17-8d9a-5b5c5ccfc105)
Virtus Pro beat MIBR there and we can see that the event weight is 0.143, so we can deduct the prize pool of this event was 0$ or 1$ in the calculation and thus the minimum value of 1$ was used.

To find out how this happened we need to look at where the data comes from: (HLTV)

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/7fb6e905-ca0d-48e0-a74b-cde0d00ea51f)
Now its getting interesting: As we can see, there was indeed some prize money won. 28,000$ in total. But what HLTV sees as the real prize pool are the "IEM Katowice 2025 spots". This string will be delivered in the data file as the prize pool of the event as we can see in the sample data from 2023:

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/b7017fa2-2b73-437e-99bd-ef14e6c6937b)
And the current code sets the prize pool to 0, if the value given for a prize pool cannot be parsed to a number like in this example.
In reality with a prize pool of 28,000$ the event weight should be 0.392.

There are two possible solutions:

- HLTV only reports the money won by teams in an event as the prize pool and never a string like "spots in the main event"
- (probably better solution). In the data loader always calculate the prize pool of an event as the sum of all the winnings from all teams as they are also reported in the data

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c9baf9d1-1261-457b-beab-e01135aef8c4)

Additionally one could imagine that its in the intent of the ranking, also to allocate some prize for the qualification teams in the calculation, because they have not won any money yet, but with their qualification they have secured a minimum winning in the main event. The minimum winning in the IEM Kato main event was 10,000$. Would we allocate this to the prize pool of the Play-in, the total Play-in prize pool would be 108,000$, which would lead to a event weight of 0.508, which is also much more in line which the actual importance of the Play-in in my opinion.

title: Cash flow statement: "Cash at beginning of period" is always $0.00
body_excerpt:
## Bug description

The cash flow statement report (`GET /api/reports/cashflow-statement`) always
shows **$0.00** for "Cash at beginning of period" — and consequently a wrong
"Cash at end of period" — regardless of how much cash activity exists before
the report window. The operating/investing/financing sections compute
correctly; only the beginning/ending cash lines are wrong.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Create any cash/bank transaction dated **before** the report window — e.g.
   a published manual journal dated 2025-12-31 debiting a bank account
   $10,000, or any earlier deposit.
2. Request the cash flow statement for a window starting after it:
   `GET /api/reports/cashflow-statement?from_date=2026-01-01&to_date=2026-12-31`
   (same result in the web UI).
3. "Cash at beginning of period" shows $0.00. Expected: $10,000.00.

The result is $0.00 for **any** `from_date` — the prior balance never appears.
Other reports (trial balance, balance sheet, general ledger) carry the same
prior balances forward correctly, so the data is fine; only this report's
beginning-cash line is affected.

## Root cause

The beginning-cash ledger is built from dateless SQL aggregation rows and then
filtered by date in memory, which drops every row:

1. `CashFlowRepository.cashAtBeginningTotalTransactions`
   (`packages/server/src/modules/FinancialStatements/modules/CashFlowStatement/CashFlowRepository.ts`,
   ~line 58) builds the query with the `creditDebitSummation` modifier —
   `SUM(credit), SUM(debit)` grouped by `accountId`, **no date column
   selected** (`packages/server/src/modules/Accounts/models/AccountTransaction.model.ts`,
   ~line 201). The date bound is applied here, in SQL
   (`filterDateRange(null, fromDate - 1 day)`), which is correct.

2. The resulting rows become a `Ledger` whose entries have `entry.date ===
   undefined` (`CashFlowService.ts` — `Ledger.fromTransactions(cashAtBeginningTransactions)`).

3. `CashFlow.cashAccountMetaMapper`
   (`packages/server/src/modules/FinancialStatements/modules/CashFlowStatement/CashFlow.ts`,
   ~line 379) then filters that ledger **again** by date:

   ```ts
   const closingBalance = this.cashLedger
     .whereToDate(cashToDate)   // <-- redundant; SQL already bounded the dates
     .whereAccountId(account.id)
     .getClosingBalance();
   ```

4. `Ledger#whereToDate` (`packages/server/src/modules/Ledger/Ledger.ts`, ~line 85):

   ```ts
   return this.filter(
     (entry) =>
       toDateParsed.isAfter(entry.date) || toDateParsed.isSame(entry.date),
   );
   ```

   With `entry.date === undefined`, both `moment#isAfter(undefined)` and
   `moment#isSame(undefined)` return `false` (comparison against an invalid
   moment), so **every** beginning-cash entry is filtered out and the closing
   balance is always 0.

## Suggested fix

Either:

- Remove the redundant `.whereToDate(cashToDate)` in
  `cashAccountMetaMapper` — the beginning-cash ledger is already bounded to
  `fromDate - 1 day` by `filterDateRange` in SQL;

title: Persist dual-leg product/cash pairing completeness and mismatch evidence
body_excerpt:
## Problem
The shared dual-leg accounting model requires position-level transactions with cash impact to have linked product and cash legs. The current model has linkage fields, but the pairing completeness and mismatch state should be persisted and queryable as first-class evidence.

## Evidence
- `docs/rfc-transaction-specs/shared/13-dual-leg-accounting-and-cash-adjustment-model.md` makes linked product/cash legs mandatory for BUY, SELL, DIVIDEND, INTEREST, and similar position-level transactions with cash impact.
- `Transaction` has nullable fields such as `economic_event_id`, `linked_transaction_group_id`, `originating_transaction_id`, `linked_cash_transaction_id`, `link_type`, and `reconciliation_key`.
- The same standard says a valid product leg without a corresponding cash leg is incomplete unless explicitly parked, and the same applies to a cash leg without a product leg.

## Why this matters
If product and cash legs are not paired deterministically, cash balances, performance flows, and reconciliation can double count or miss economic effects. Support teams also need to know whether a missing leg is expected, pending, rejected, or inconsistent.

## Suggested direction
- Add a pairing/economic-event ledger that records expected legs, received legs, matched legs, mismatch reasons, and completion state.
- Validate product/cash signs, net amount, currency, settlement account, and originating transaction links.
- Expose incomplete or mismatched pairs through supportability APIs.
- Treat parked incomplete pairs as a governed lifecycle state.

## Acceptance criteria
- Product/cash leg completeness is persisted per economic event or linked transaction group.
- Missing, duplicate, wrong-sign, wrong-currency, and wrong-account pairs are detectable.

title: Bug: "Recent Tournament Events" displays hardcoded placeholder data instead of real completed tournaments
body_excerpt:
## Summary

The \"Recent Tournament Events\" section on the dashboard always shows two hardcoded dummy events from September 2025 instead of fetching real completed tournament data from the backend.

## Root Cause

In `src/pages/index.tsx` (line 110), the `<RecentEvents>` component is called with the exported `dummyEvents` constant:

```tsx
// src/pages/index.tsx:4
import { dummyEvents } from "../utils/types/events";

// src/pages/index.tsx:110
<RecentEvents events={dummyEvents} />
```

The `getServerSideProps` function (lines 252–405) fetches all 6 active leaderboards and prizes in parallel, but **never calls the backend endpoint that returns recent completed tournament data**. The same issue exists in `src/pages/dashboard.tsx:39` and `src/pages/leaderboard.tsx` (which even has a `// TODO: Figure out how to actually fetch events later` comment).

The two hardcoded placeholder events in `src/utils/types/events.ts` are:
- "Single Player Daily Tournament" — September 17, 2025
- "Multiplayer Daily Tournament" — September 18, 2025

## Backend API Available

The backend already supports this via `GET /api/v2/tournament/summary?includeWinners=true`, which returns a `recentWinners` array from `TournamentService.getRecentMetadata()`. That method queries the `tournament_metadata` table for the 10 most recent completed tournaments (status = `'completed'`, `winningTime != null`), ordered by `endDate DESC`.

`tournamentApi.getTournamentSummary()` already exists in `src/services/tournamentApi.ts` and can be used to call this endpoint.

## Fix

In `getServerSideProps` in `src/pages/index.tsx`:
1. Add a call to `tournamentApi.getTournamentSummary({ includeWinners: true })` in the `Promise.all` block.
2. Map the `recentWinners` response to the `TournamentEvent[]` shape expected by `<RecentEvents>`.
3. Pass the real events to `<RecentEvents>` instead of `dummyEvents`.
4. Apply the same fix to `dashboard.tsx` and `leaderboard.tsx`.
5. Remove or deprecate `dummyEvents` from `src/utils/types/events.ts` once real data is wired up.

## Files Affected

- `src/pages/index.tsx` — line 4 (import), line 110 (usage), `getServerSideProps` (no fetch)
- `src/pages/dashboard.tsx` — line 39
- `src/pages/leaderboard.tsx`
- `src/utils/types/events.ts` — `dummyEvents` constant to be removed
- `src/services/tournamentApi.ts` — `getTournamentSummary()` already exists, just needs to be called

title: Improve challenge onboarding and explain Fair Rewards
body_excerpt:
## Problem

New participants can see challenge cards and point values, but the product does not yet explain the Fair Rewards model clearly enough inside the app:

- what challenges are;
- how they are evaluated;
- what pending vs completed means;
- why some challenges need review or external proof;
- how challenge progress translates into points and profile reputation.

This creates avoidable uncertainty, especially when users encounter their first task or when progress is not instantly awarded.

## Proposal

Add a lightweight challenge onboarding experience that teaches the basics before users start earning.

A simple first version could be a default onboarding challenge:

- user opens a short explainer from the Challenges feed;
- explainer covers challenge mechanics, progress states, review, and rewards;
- user answers a few simple questions to confirm understanding;
- completing it qualifies the user for a small starter reward or completion state.

This should feel like part of the Fair Rewards system, not a detached help page.

## Why

The challenge UI is becoming more dynamic and status-rich. To make that useful, users need a shared mental model for what the states mean and what action is expected from them.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Challenges screen has an intentional entry point for first-time challenge education.
- Users can understand pending, completed, in-progress, and not-done states without relying on Discord context.
- The flow explains that some points may require agent/admin verification before completion.
- The onboarding challenge can be represented by the same challenge/detail components used elsewhere.
- Copy is user-facing and plain-language, not implementation or backend terminology.

title: check_sample_adequacy verdicts every multi-repo/generalization run INADEQUATE: _decided reads only a top-level tally that cross-repo runs never emit
body_excerpt:
### What happened?

`check_sample_adequacy` gates whether a run "judged and accounted for enough tasks" — its
`all_tasks_decided` check verifies the challenger/baseline/tie tally sums to the task total, so no
task vanished between judging and tallying. Its `_total_tasks` helper is multi-repo aware (it sums
each `per_repo` entry's `tasks` across `_partition_entries`), but its sibling `_decided` reads the
tally from **one place only** — `result.get("tally")` (top-level).

`run_multi_replay` / `run_generalization_report` artifacts have **no top-level `tally`**: the
per-task tally lives under each `per_repo[i]["tally"]` (the aggregate is under `judge_report`). So
for **every** real multi-repo / generalization run, `_decided` returns `None`, `all_tasks_decided`
fails closed, and the run is verdicted **INADEQUATE** — even when every task was decided. Since the
module's job is to stop an inadequate sample from flowing into `compare_eval` / `trend` / a
leaderboard "as if it were as solid as a full run," this permanently flags every cross-repo and M3
generalization run.

The existing tests miss it because they only reach `all_tasks_decided` passing by injecting a
**synthetic top-level `tally`** (`dict(_multi(...), tally={...})`) — a shape real runs never emit.

### Steps to reproduce

```shell
python - <<'PY'
from benchmark.sample_adequacy import check_sample_adequacy, _total_tasks, _decided
# real run_multi_replay shape: no top-level tally; per_repo carries the tallies
multi = {"per_repo": [
    {"repo": "a", "tasks": 5, "tally": {"challenger": 4, "baseline": 1, "tie": 0}},
    {"repo": "b", "tasks": 5, "tally": {"challenger": 3, "baseline": 1, "tie": 1}},
]}
print("total_tasks:", _total_tasks(multi))   # 10 (correct)
print("decided:", _decided(multi))           # bug: None
print("passed:", check_sample_adequacy(multi)["passed"])  # bug: False (INADEQUATE)
PY
```

### Area

benchmark (freeze / taskgen / judge / runner)

### Python version

3.11

### Relevant logs or output

```shell
total_tasks: 10
decided: None
passed: False
```

title: Economic e2e: assert reward/slash state transitions through block processing
body_excerpt:
The economic contracts (emissions, ordering rewards, slashing) are well covered **in-process** (lite property tests via `Signer::Core`), but no test asserts an economic state transition through a real/simulated **block-processing** path. `distribute_ordering_reward`, `slash`, and `slash_equivocation` currently have **zero production callers** — the reactor produces consensus decisions, the contracts compute rewards/penalties, and nothing connects them.

**Gap:** the failure→slash loop and reward accrual are untested end-to-end. The PoR regtest e2e proves valid proofs only (no slash on challenge failure); consensus tests assert anchors/checkpoints but never a payout.

**Blocked on:** the reactor↔economics wiring (#442) — once block boundaries call the distribute/slash/emit paths, add regtest `#[testlib::test]` cases that:
- drive ordered batches through a mined block and assert validator stake grew by the ordering emission, and
- let a challenge expire unproven, mine, and assert the offender's stake was slashed and redistributed.

The cross-feature invariant harness (token conservation, `total_active_stake == Σ stakes`, slash conservation, cross-indexer determinism via the checkpoint hash-chain) is the deterministic-sim suite (#444).

**Already done:** the user-driven slice — storage creation-fee burn asserted through block processing — landed in #460. This issue tracks the consensus-driven remainder.

title: [Hackathon] Width-aware progress ticker
body_excerpt:
### Discord Username / User ID

interferon0

### What does this improvement do?

The test run --wait / test wait progress ticker prints a single in-place line. On a narrow terminal or with a long run id the line soft-wraps to a second row, and the next \x1b[2K\r clears only one of the two rows, corrupting the redraw (ghost lines). This clips each frame to the current terminal width, re-read on every poll so it also follows a live resize. It stays completely silent on non-TTY (CI) and under --output json, so machine output is unchanged.

### Details / implementation notes

Approach: width-aware truncation in src/lib/ticker.ts (read process.stderr.columns ?? 80, clip to width-1 to avoid last-cell auto-wrap, append a 1-column ellipsis). No new dependencies (ticker content is ASCII, so .length is an exact column count). Adds 10 unit tests (truncation, simulated resize, 80-col fallback, non-TTY silence). Full gate green: tsc, eslint, prettier, 1703 tests, coverage 98% on ticker.ts. PR to follow once assigned.

title: view scores at specified point in time
body_excerpt:
We're currently always presenting "today's" leaderboard.
But for references, it might often be useful to point at the state of the leaderboard at some point in the past.
For instance, for the 2019 CORnet paper, we might want to point to the model scores at the time. Similarly, a new paper might want to point out its state-of-the-art scores at the time of submission/publication.

Challenges:
* we do not have a timestamp of when we set benchmarks to public, so going back in time might show scores from benchmarks that were private at the time, i.e. did not show up on the leaderboard. If grouping ever changes, then we also do currently not have any way to keep track of that. I wonder if it would be better to just store the entire website each day, rather than doing this via database timestamps
* ideally we'd like to highlight certain points in time, e.g. "2020 Neuron paper", "before 2022 competition" etc. How can we design this?

title: Rename project fields date fields so they aren't confusing
body_excerpt:
Currently, projects have 2 fields besides start date:
- Close date: The date the tournament wraps up and prizes will be paid. All questions that should be included in the leaderboard must close and resolve before this date. This is displayed on the front end as the “Winners announced date”
- Forecasting end date: The date the last scored question that counts for the tournament closes. The date shown is the latest of the Forecasting end date and the latest question close date closing and resolving before the Close date.

The Forecasting end date is labelled "Closes" on the front end.

We should rename Close date to “Winners announced date” and Forecasting end date to "Close date".

title: Feature Request: Gamified Productivity Rankings and Leaderboards
body_excerpt:
# Feature Description

Implement a gamification system that introduces productivity leaderboards and rankings for users based on their consistency and task completion.

---

# Problem Statement

Maintaining long-term consistency can be challenging without external motivation. Users currently rely solely on intrinsic motivation and personal streaks, which may not be enough to prevent burnout or habit abandonment over time.

---

# Proposed Solution

Develop a point-based system where users earn experience points (XP) for completing tasks, maintaining habit streaks, and finishing projects. Include a global or friends-only leaderboard where users can compare their productivity scores to foster a sense of community and healthy competition.

---

# Possible Alternatives

1. A purely individual reward system (e.g., unlocking badges) without any social comparison or leaderboards.
2. Keeping the platform strictly private without any gamification features.

---

# Additional Context

This feature supports the "Community & Engagement" roadmap goal and will help increase user retention by making goal execution more engaging and rewarding.

title: P0: Rebuild cash-in and cash-out state machines
body_excerpt:
## Problem
Speedcash still needs production-safe money state machines. Cash-in must not create spendable balance before trusted provider proof. Cash-out must use available/hold states and complete only after verified provider success.

## Risk
Unauthorized credits, misstated funds, stranded holds, and failed settlement accounting.

## Files likely affected
- `functions/src/transactions/handlers.ts`
- `functions/src/admin/handlers.ts`
- new Money Core service files
- provider adapter files
- state-machine tests

## Acceptance criteria
- Cash-in request creates pending provider-confirmation state only.
- Cash-in credit happens only after verified provider event or trusted status poll.
- Cash-out request reserves funds into hold state.
- Admin approval does not mark transaction complete.
- Provider success completes; provider failure reverses hold.
- All transitions are idempotent.

## Tests required
- Cash-in duplicate reference tests.
- Cash-in no-credit-before-proof tests.
- Cash-out hold/success/failure/reversal tests.
- State-transition unit tests.

## Docs
See `docs/production-readiness/05_MONEY_MOVEMENT_STATE_MACHINES.md` and `14_PRODUCTION_GO_NO_GO_CHECKLIST.md`.

title: Receipts screen: Z-report day totals with Cash and Card breakdown
body_excerpt:
## Summary

On the **Receipts** screen, each calendar day already shows a single **Total** footer after the last receipt for that day (`ReceiptList.withDayTotals` in `core/`). Volunteers also need to see how much of that daily total was paid **cash** vs **card** — for end-of-day cash reconciliation.

Show a **Z-report style** breakdown under each day total: **Total**, then **Cash** and **Card** as indented sub-lines. Always show all three amounts, including `$0.00` when a payment method had no sales that day.

## User story

As a nursery volunteer reviewing the day’s sales on the Receipts screen, I want to see the total takings for each day and how much was cash vs card, so I can reconcile the cash drawer without mental arithmetic.

## Problem (current behaviour)

- `ReceiptListItem.DayTotal` carries only `totalCents`.
- `DayTotalRow` in `ReceiptsScreen.kt` renders one line: `"{date} Total: $X"`.
- Each `Receipt` already records `paymentMethod: PaymentMethod` (`CARD` / `CASH`) and the line totals are computed with `Money.receiptTotalCents`, but the day footer does not use payment method.

## Proposed behaviour

After the last receipt card for a calendar day, show a Z-report block (right-aligned, visually grouped):

```
3 July 2026
Total          $125.50
  Cash          $40.00
  Card          $85.50
```

Rules:

1. **Total** = sum of all receipts that day (unchanged — includes pending + exported, even when waterline grouping splits them).
2. **Cash** = sum of receipt totals where `paymentMethod == CASH`.
3. **Card** = sum of receipt totals where `paymentMethod == CARD`.
4. **Always show Cash and Card**, even when `$0.00`.
5. Cash and Card are **parts of** Total (not added on top). Visual hierarchy: date → Total (`titleMedium`, bold) → indented Cash/Card (`bodyLarge` or slightly lighter).
6. No backend / export / DB schema changes — `paymentMethod` is already persisted on receipts.

## Scope

### In scope

- `core/ReceiptList.kt`: extend `DayTotal` with `cashCents` and `cardCents`; compute in `withDayTotals`.
- `core/ReceiptListTest.kt`: tests for mixed days, all-cash, all-card, zero lines, pending+exported same day.
- `app/.../ReceiptsScreen.kt`: Z-report layout for `DayTotalRow`.

### Out of scope

- Per-receipt payment display changes (already on detail + confirm screens).
- Split-tender / partial cash+card on one receipt (not a domain concept today).
- Hiding zero payment-method lines.
- SQL aggregation in Room or logic in the ViewModel.

## Implementation sketch

### 1. `core/ReceiptList.kt`

```kotlin
data class DayTotal(
    val epochDay: Long,
    val totalCents: Long,
    val cashCents: Long,
    val cardCents: Long,
)
```

In `withDayTotals`, when grouping receipts by local calendar day:

- `totalCents` — existing sum over all receipts.
- `cashCents` — sum `Money.receiptTotalCents(lines)` for `paymentMethod == CASH`.
- `cardCents` — same for `CARD`.

Invariant: `cashCents + cardCents == totalCents` (only two payment methods exist).

### 2

title: Clarify or wire offline fallback/challenger model behavior
body_excerpt:
## Context

The model-selection decision and env surface describe fallback/challenger models for offline classify/fill, but the code does not currently route those fallbacks through OpenRouter.

Relevant code:

- `pipeline/classify.py` defines `FALLBACK_MODEL = "z-ai/glm-5.1"`, but `resolve_classify_model()` only reads `CLASSIFY_MODEL` and the OpenRouter call sends a single `model`.
- `pipeline/fill.py` defines `FALLBACK_MODEL = "z-ai/glm-5.1"`, but `resolve_fill_model()` only reads `FILL_MODEL` and the OpenRouter call sends a single `model`.
- `.env.example` documents `CLASSIFY_FALLBACK_MODEL` and `FILL_FALLBACK_MODEL` as configurable fallback/challenger values.

## Why this matters

There are two different concepts being mixed:

- **fallback**: provider/model used automatically when primary is unavailable;
- **challenger**: model used deliberately in an eval or A/B pass, not in production fallback routing.

The docs and variable names imply automatic fallback, but jobs 3/4 currently do not pass OpenRouter `models` or equivalent fallback routing. That mismatch will surprise anyone operating the kiosk.

## Suggested fix

Either:

1. wire true fallback routing for classify/fill, using OpenRouter's supported `models`/provider fallback body and tests; or
2. rename the env/docs to challenger-only (`CLASSIFY_CHALLENGER_MODEL`, `FILL_CHALLENGER_MODEL`) and keep production calls single-model until G17 evaluates challengers.

I lean toward option 2 unless there is a concrete failure mode where automatic fallback is wanted; for the authoritative sort, silent fallback can change quality characteristics.

## Acceptance criteria

- Env names, docs, code, and Decision 0001 agree on whether GLM is fallback or challenger.
- Tests assert the request body for classify/fill model routing.
- `.env.example` no longer promises behavior that is not wired.

title: 4 New submissions for Wed, 31 Jan 24
body_excerpt:
## Keyword: chest
### Category-wise Fine-Tuning: Resisting Incorrect Pseudo-Labels in  Multi-Label Image Classification with Partial Labels
 - **Authors:** Chak Fong Chong, Xinyi Fang, Jielong Guo, Yapeng Wang, Wei Ke, Chan-Tong Lam, Sio-Kei Im
 - **Subjects:** Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
 - **Arxiv link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.16991
 - **Pdf link:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.16991
 - **Abstract**
 Large-scale image datasets are often partially labeled, where only a few categories' labels are known for each image. Assigning pseudo-labels to unknown labels to gain additional training signals has become prevalent for training deep classification models. However, some pseudo-labels are inevitably incorrect, leading to a notable decline in the model classification performance. In this paper, we propose a novel method called Category-wise Fine-Tuning (CFT), aiming to reduce model inaccuracies caused by the wrong pseudo-labels. In particular, CFT employs known labels without pseudo-labels to fine-tune the logistic regressions of trained models individually to calibrate each category's model predictions. Genetic Algorithm, seldom used for training deep models, is also utilized in CFT to maximize the classification performance directly. CFT is applied to well-trained models, unlike most existing methods that train models from scratch. Hence, CFT is general and compatible with models trained with different methods and schemes, as demonstrated through extensive experiments. CFT requires only a few seconds for each category for calibration with consumer-grade GPUs. We achieve state-of-the-art results on three benchmarking datasets, including the CheXpert chest X-ray competition dataset (ensemble mAUC 93.33%, single model 91.82%), partially labeled MS-COCO (average mAP 83.69%), and Open Image V3 (mAP 85.31%), outperforming the previous bests by 0.28%, 2.21%, 2.50%, and 0.91%, respectively. title: verify_submission_result matches challenge summary by hash only, allowing cross-submission reuse
body_excerpt:
## Summary

`verify_submission_result()` (`kata/submissions.py`) treats a challenge result as belonging to the submission under verification when only these match:

1. `summary.mode == validation.metadata.mode`
2. `summary.candidate_artifact_hash == hash_submission_bundle(submission_path)`

It does **not** check that `summary.candidate_artifact` resolves to the same path as `submission_path`, nor that lane `challenge_state.candidate_submission_id` matches `validation.metadata.submission_id`.

Because artifact hashing is content-only, two different submission directories with identical `agent.py` produce the same hash. A PR can point `verify`/`decide`/`promote` at submission B while supplying `challenge_summary.json` from submission A's winning run. If king/benchmark are still current, `auto_merge_ready` becomes true and the wrong submission can be promoted.

This breaks the documented auto-merge invariant: *"Before a merge, the result is re-checked against the current submission payload."* Hash equality is necessary but not sufficient.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Run a winning duel for submission A under `submissions/<pack>/<mode>/alice-.../`.
2. Copy the same `agent.py` into a second submission B with a different `submission_id` (same content hash).
3. Call `verify_submission_result(str(submission_B), summary_path_from_A)`.

## Expected behavior

Verification fails: `submission_matches_challenge` is false and `auto_merge_ready` is false because the challenge summary was produced for a different submission identity.

## Actual behavior

Verification succeeds when hashes match, even though `summary.candidate_artifact` and lane `candidate_submission_id` refer to submission A.

## Context

`ChallengeSummary` already records `candidate_artifact` (path), and lane `ChallengeState` records `candidate_submission_id` — both are unused during verification. `tests/test_submissions.py` covers stale benchmark/king cases but not cross-submission hash collision. Per `CONTRIBUTING.md`, this is an evaluator correctness / promotion safety issue.

PR to follow.

title: [2606.27666v1] MultModLM: A multi-modal benchmark for Large-Language Model based hardware schematic generation
body_excerpt:
## MultModLM: A multi-modal benchmark for Large-Language Model based hardware schematic generation

**Authors:** Dhruv Kulkarni, Sai Manoj Pudukotai Dinkarrao
**Published:** 2026-06-26
**Categories:** `cs.AR`

**Links:** [abs](http://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27666v1) | [pdf](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.27666v1)

---

### Abstract

Recently, Large Language models (LLMs) find application in several fields. This extends to hardware definition and synthesis. However, most works at the intersection of LLMs and hardware generation focus on text-based tasks, creating a gap for multi-modal LLMs for RTL design. In this work, we introduce MultModLM, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on the task of generating hardware schematics from RTL (Register Transfer Level) descriptions. The dataset consists of 99 diverse RTL modules spanning arithmetic, control, and state-based designs. To address the challenges of non-unique schematic representations, we propose a multi-stage evaluation framework combining rubric-based scoring, self-evaluation, cross-model assessment, blind evaluation, and human validation to enable exhaustive evaluation.
  Through experiments on state-of-the-art LLMs, we observe that while models can generate visually interpretable schematics, their functional correctness remains constrained. Furthermore, we find that LLM-based evaluators exhibit near-zero agreement with human raters, revealing, as a key finding, that LLM-as-a-judge paradigms are unreliable in structurally precise domains. These findings suggest that reliable evaluation of multi-modal hardware outputs remains an open challenge, motivating the need for more robust and domain-aware evaluation methodologies, as well as tools for structural evaluation, so as to enable formal equivalence checkers.

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    EVOLUTION MEMORY SYSTEM                          │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤

title: The Tour de France
body_excerpt:
The Tour de France is an annual multiple stage bicycle race primarily held in France, while also occasionally making passes through nearby countries. The race was first organized in 1903 to increase paper sales for the magazine L’Auto; it is currently run by the Amaury Sport Organisation. The race has been held annually since its first edition in 1903 except when it was stopped for the two World Wars (1915-1919; 1940-1947). As the Tour gained prominence and popularity the race was lengthened and its reach began to extend around the globe. Participation expanded from a primarily French field, as riders from all over the world began to participate in the race each year. The Tour is a UCI World Tour event, which means that the teams that compete in the race are mostly UCI ProTeams, with the exception of the teams that the organizers invite.
The Tour de France, the Giro d’Italia and Vuelta a España make up cycling’s prestigious, three-week-long Grand Tours; the Tour is the oldest and generally considered the most prestigious of the three. Traditionally, the race is held primarily in the month of July. While the route changes each year, the format of the race stays the same with the appearance of time trials, the passage through the mountain chains of the Pyrenees and the Alps, and the finish on the Champs-Élysées in Paris. The modern editions of the Tour de France consist of 21 day-long segments (stages) over a 23-day period and cover around 3,500 kilometres (2,200 mi). The 2014 edition consisted of 9 flat stages, 5 hilly stages, 6 mountain stages with 5 high-altitude finishes, and 1 individual time-trial stage. The race alternates between clockwise and anticlockwise circuits of France.
The number of teams usually varies between 20 and 22, with nine riders in each. All of the stages are timed to the finish; after finishing the riders’ times are compounded with their previous stage times. The rider with the lowest aggregate time is the leader of the race and gets to don the coveted yellow jersey. title: Add explicit maximum length checks for packed custom share arrays
body_excerpt:
## Summary

Packed custom share storage uses `u8` slot indexes. With 15 shares per slot, the practical maximum is 3,840 shares. Larger arrays panic through `try_into().unwrap()` instead of failing with a clear validation error.

## Affected Code

- `packages/metagame/src/prize/prize_store.cairo:184`
- `packages/metagame/src/prize/prize_store.cairo:102`
- `packages/utilities/src/distribution/packed_shares.cairo:100`
- `packages/utilities/src/distribution/packed_shares.cairo:107`

## Risk

Configuration failure and poor error behavior for oversized custom distributions.

## Suggested Fix

Define a max custom share count constant and reject larger arrays before storage loops.

## Suggested Tests

Add boundary tests for:

- `3840` shares succeeds
- `3841` shares reverts with a clear error

title: Audit Search by Date Range
body_excerpt:
# Audit Search by Date Range

**Request Type:** New Feature

## 👤 User Story

As a compliance officer and security analyst, I want to search audit trails within specific date ranges so that I can investigate incidents during particular time periods, generate periodic compliance reports, and analyze activity patterns over defined timeframes.

## Route URL

`/api/audit/search/by-date-range`

## 🚨 Problem Statement, Use Case, or Opportunity

Currently, there is no capability to search audit trails within specific date ranges, making it difficult to investigate time-based incidents, generate periodic compliance reports, analyze activity trends over specific periods, and perform forensic analysis for particular timeframes.

## 💡 Proposed Solution

Implement comprehensive date range-based audit search functionality:

- Flexible date range selection with multiple input formats
- Predefined time period shortcuts (last 24 hours, week, month)
- Timezone support for accurate time-based searches
- Date range validation and boundary checks
- Performance optimization for large date range queries
- Time-based aggregation and trending analysis
- Relative date range support ("last N days")
- Date range export and reporting capabilities

title: Surprisingly fast pure Python cycle basis: Beats igraph C-core on grid graphs
body_excerpt:
Body
Hi igraph team,

I've developed a pure Python (stdlib only, zero dependencies) implementation for extracting full-rank chordless cycle bases. I'm sharing this here because igraph's MCB implementation has been my primary benchmark, and I'm eager to get feedback from experts in this domain.

What it does
Given an undirected graph, it extracts a set of algebraically independent, chordless cycles that span the cycle space (rank = E − V + C). The algorithm relies on edge-based expansion with collision elimination, diverging from the traditional shortest spanning tree approach.

Why it exists
I entered a competition requiring pure Python (no C extensions allowed). Combined with my lack of C++ expertise, I had to roll my own instead of forking igraph. The result is a library deployable anywhere Python runs, with no compilation needed.

Benchmark results
Tested against igraph's MCB on 20 synthetic graphs (5k–10k edges), including dense short-cycle, grid, and mixed long-cycle topologies. All datasets passed full-rank audits (100% rank alignment, 0 chordal cycles).

Where it wins: Pure 4-cycle grid graphs
On uniform grid topologies, the edge-expansion approach scales better than the spanning tree method. The performance advantage grows with graph size, overcoming Python's inherent runtime overhead.
Dataset   V / E / Rank   igraph (C)   Blackhole Diffusion (Python)   Speedup
edge007   2500 / 4900 / 2401   8.70s   5.56s   1.57×
edge017   4900 / 9660 / 4761   52.82s   23.38s   2.26×

Where igraph wins: Mixed/Long-cycle graphs
As expected, igraph is generally 5–17× faster on most graph types due to the C vs. Python difference. Micro-benchmarks show a baseline "~15× language tax" from Python's runtime (object allocation, GC, interpreter loop).
Dataset   V / E / Rank   Topology   igraph   BH   Ratio
edge003   1666 / 4989 / 3324   Mixed 3–7 cycle   2.88s   43.82s   15.2×
edge014   2000 / 9975 / 7976   Mixed 3–6 cycle   10.86s   181.94s   16.8×

MCB Accuracy
*   Exact Match (35%): 7 out of 20 datasets match igraph's MCB total edge count exactly (all dense short-cycle/pure grid graphs with MCB ≤ 5).
*   Drift: On longer-cycle graphs, total edge count inflates by 1–46% (cycle length drift +1 to +8).

Questions for the community
1.  Algorithmic Observation: Is the grid-graph speedup pattern (edge expansion outperforming spanning tree on uniform local structure) a known property, or has this been observed before?
2.  Benchmarks: Are there standard benchmark graph sets for cycle basis algorithms? I used synthetic data but would prefer established suites.
3.  Related Work: Without a formal graph theory background, I developed this independently (avoiding Horton/de Pina/Kavitha families). Can anyone point me to related literature?

Links
- Repository: - - https://github.com/m15154178071-cmyk/blackhole-diffusion
- MIT licensed

Thanks for building igraph—it's the gold standard I used for validation.

title: F9: Formal verification integration
body_excerpt:
## Vision

Prove code is correct, not just test it. Mathematical certainty for critical code paths. Automatically generated counterexamples.

## The Problem

Testing is empirical:
- Shows code works for tested inputs
- Can't prove absence of bugs
- Edge cases often missed
- 100% coverage ≠ 100% correct

Critical code (crypto, auth, financial) needs stronger guarantees.

## Design

### Verification interface
```go
type FormalVerifier struct {
    Prover ProverBackend  // Z3, Dafny, Coq, etc.
}

type VerificationResult struct {
    Property     string
    Status       string  // "proven", "counterexample", "timeout", "unknown"
    Proof        string  // Human-readable proof sketch
    CounterEx    *CounterExample
    Duration     time.Duration
}

type Property struct {
    Name        string
    Description string
    Assertion   string  // Formal specification
}

type CounterExample struct {
    Inputs   map[string]interface{}
    Trace    []Step
    Violated string  // Which property
}
```

### Example flow
```
User: "Prove this sorting function is correct"

Agent: Analyzing `quickSort(arr []int) []int`...

Properties to verify:
1. Output is permutation of input
2. Output is sorted (∀i: result[i] ≤ result[i+1])
3. Function terminates

Results:

✅ Property 1: PROVEN
   Function only swaps elements, preserving multiset.

✅ Property 2: PROVEN
   Partition invariant maintained, induction on size.

⚠️ Property 3: UNPROVEN
   Termination depends on pivot selection.

   Counterexample:
   - Input: [5, 4, 3, 2, 1] (descending)
   - Pivot: always rightmost (max element)
   - Result: recursion depth = n, stack overflow possible

   Fix: Use median-of-three pivot selection.

[Apply fix] [Show proof details] [Ignore warning]
```

### Property templates
```go
var CommonProperties = []PropertyTemplate{
    {Name: "no_null_deref", Spec: "∀ptr. deref(ptr) → ptr ≠ null"},
    {Name: "bounds_check", Spec: "∀arr,i. access(arr,i) → 0 ≤ i < len(arr)"},
    {Name: "no_overflow", Spec: "∀a,b. add(a,b) → MIN ≤ a+b ≤ MAX"},
    {Name: "termination", Spec: "∃variant. variant decreases ∧ variant ≥ 0"},
}
```

## What This Enables

- Mathematical certainty for critical code
- Catch edge cases tests miss
- Prove absence of bug classes
- Auto-generate counterexamples
- Security property verification
- Compliance proofs

## Implementation Approach

1. **Phase 1**: Integration with Z3 for simple assertions
2. **Phase 2**: Property template library
3. **Phase 3**: Automatic property inference
4. **Phase 4**: Counterexample visualization
5. **Phase 5**: Proof-carrying code

## Open Questions

- Which prover backend(s)?
- Annotation syntax for properties?
- How to handle undecidable properties?
- Balance between automation and manual specs?

## Technical Challenges

- SMT solver integration
- Property specification language
- Proof explanation in plain English
- Performance for large functions
- Handling external dependencies

## References

- Z3 (SMT solver)
- Dafny (verificatio

title: Harden runtime worker sandbox toward allow-list isolation
body_excerpt:
## Problem
The runtime worker sandbox currently uses a deny-list profile: `(allow default)` with explicit denies for network, process fork/exec, file writes, and private golden/prompt paths. This is good enough for the current prompt-exfiltration threat model, but it is not a fully tight isolation boundary for high-effort adversaries.

## Current defenses
- Worker sandbox denies `network*`.
- Worker sandbox denies `process-fork` and `process-exec*`, except the trusted benchmark binary itself.
- Worker sandbox denies `file-write*`, except `/dev/null`.
- Worker sandbox denies reads of the private correctness golden file and `MLXFAST_PRIVATE_DIR`.
- Current profiles do **not** explicitly allow localhost or Unix sockets.

## Residual risk
- `(allow default)` means anything not explicitly denied remains available, including broad filesystem reads outside private prompt paths and some OS IPC/Mach surfaces.
- Seatbelt is not a perfect security boundary, especially across OS versions.
- If we later raise the adversarial bar, this profile should move closer to a tested allow-list rather than relying on deny-list rules.

## Proposed hardening
- Build a stricter runtime-worker Seatbelt profile that starts from denied default behavior and explicitly allows only what MLX/Metal/CoreFoundation/model execution actually needs.
- Validate it on the official Blacksmith macOS runner and representative local Apple Silicon machines.
- Add regression tests that assert the profile blocks network, process creation, writes, private prompt/golden reads, localhost/Unix socket access, and representative unexpected filesystem reads.
- Keep benchmark correctness/score behavior unchanged while tightening the OS surface.

## Notes
This should not block the current benchmark hardening work. Treat it as production hardening before promoting the harness to a high-adversary public competition.

title: Isabelle/HOL compute planning for AFP: session build times are orders of magnitude heavier than Coq
body_excerpt:
## Context

The 2026-06-22 meeting scoped Matthew's 120GB RAM / 64-core machine for type-checking Lean/Coq solutions in the git-history evals pipeline.

## Problem

Isabelle/HOL session builds are dramatically more expensive than Coq or Lean compilation. seL4's Isabelle session alone takes several hours on capable hardware. AFP theories often import deep transitive dependency chains, meaning a single challenge's grader may need to rebuild a large portion of the session heap.

This is qualitatively different from the Coq/Lean workload already budgeted for Matthew's machine.

## Questions to resolve

- What is the build time profile for a representative AFP theory (e.g. a mid-sized HOL-Algebra entry)?
- Can session heaps be pre-built and cached per AFP entry, or do ablations invalidate the heap?
- Is Matthew's machine sufficient, or does AFP grading require a different compute arrangement (e.g. cloud, pre-built Docker images with cached heaps)?

## Action

Before AFP goes on the milestone chart, run a benchmark: pick 3-5 AFP entries of varying sizes, time a cold Isabelle build + proof check, and document RAM/CPU usage. Use this to size the compute requirement.

title: [payment-ux] Payment page commit UX: sticky confirm bar, payment-form prominence, reserved element height
body_excerpt:
# Payment page commit UX: sticky confirm bar, payment-form prominence, reserved element height

Part of milestone **Payment Conversion & Payment Experience** (#99). From the 2026-07-03 Stripe integration audit.

## Context
The payment page is the highest-stakes step but has the weakest commit UX:
- It uses `CheckoutLayout` (`account-payment-page.tsx:67`) — not the `CheckoutFlowShell` + `CheckoutStickyActionBar` + `CheckoutMobileSummaryDisclosure` trio the checkout page uses — so on mobile "Confirm payment" is inline mid-page below six sections while one page earlier "Pay now" was sticky.
- The payment form is the **6th** `PageSection` down (`account-payment-page.tsx:306-327`); the page leads with a status timeline and fee breakdown instead of the thing the buyer came to do.
- The element mount (`MountPoint purpose="provider"`, `packages/design-system/src/primitives/layout.tsx:968`) reserves no min-height → iframe-load layout shift exactly where the user is about to type, with no skeleton.

## What to do
Adopt the checkout page's shell trio here; reorder so payment entry is the primary above-the-fold content (timeline/fee breakdown demoted to disclosure/summary); add a skeleton + reserved min-height on the provider mount.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Confirm CTA is sticky on mobile, consistent with the checkout page.
- [ ] Payment form visible without scrolling on mobile viewport (m76 breakpoints).
- [ ] No layout shift on element load (skeleton reserves height).

## Constraints
- DS-first: use existing shell primitives, no custom overrides; buyer payout-leak removal on this page is m89's — don't duplicate, rebase over it.
- Sibling worktree; `verify:static` + scoped payments tests before push; rebase onto latest main right before pushing.

title: Virtual live race events with scheduled start times and prizes
body_excerpt:
## Idea

Host scheduled virtual stair-stepper race events where users sign up in advance, race the same climb at a synchronized start time, see live leaderboard positions, and earn prizes for top finishers.

Inspired by [Tower Running](https://www.towerrunning.com/races/) — the existing real-world community of organized stair-climbing races (Empire State Building Run-Up, ICC Sears Tower, etc.). Ascend's version: same competitive event format, but you don't have to travel.

## Why it fits Ascend's positioning

- Natural extension of Live Climbs — same race mechanic, live participants instead of replay ghosts
- Reaches the tower-running-curious audience who can't travel for physical events (geography, cost, time)
- Recurring events drive retention better than push notifications — people pre-register and clear their calendar around the event
- Aligns with the "leaderboard is the conversation" framing

## Already supported (no net-new work)

- Headphone-motion live tracking
- Per-attempt replay leaderboards
- Climb catalog with real landmarks
- Bucketed split math for elapsed-time rank comparison

## Net-new work required

- Event scheduling + pre-registration UI
- Synchronized start countdown across all participants
- Live multi-user broadcast layer (vs. polling published replay rows)
- **Anti-cheat for prizes** — likely combining headphone motion + Apple Health HR + a verification window for podium finishers. Solvable, but non-trivial. This is the spicy one.
- Prize fulfillment (digital badges/avatars first; physical merch or cash later as scale supports it)

## Architectural note for now

The current `live_replay_leaderboards` data model and per-climb replay contexts should stay flexible enough to accommodate synchronized real-time entries later — not just published replays of already-completed attempts. Don't paint into a corner where every replay row is keyed to a single completed workout ID.

## Roadmap placement

v2+ — after core Live Climbs is polished and the user base is large enough to fill an event roster (rough threshold: ~50+ active climbers per landmark per event window).

## Reference

- https://www.towerrunning.com/races/

title: [2602.23092v1] Enhancing CVRP Solver through LLM-driven Automatic Heuristic Design
body_excerpt:
## Enhancing CVRP Solver through LLM-driven Automatic Heuristic Design

**Authors:** Zhuoliang Xie, Fei Liu, Zhenkun Wang, Qingfu Zhang
**Published:** 2026-02-26
**Categories:** `cs.AI`

**Links:** [abs](http://arxiv.org/abs/2602.23092v1) | [pdf](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.23092v1)

---

### Abstract

The Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP), a fundamental combinatorial optimization challenge, focuses on optimizing fleet operations under vehicle capacity constraints. While extensively studied in operational research, the NP-hard nature of CVRP continues to pose significant computational challenges, particularly for large-scale instances. This study presents AILS-AHD (Adaptive Iterated Local Search with Automatic Heuristic Design), a novel approach that leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to revolutionize CVRP solving. Our methodology integrates an evolutionary search framework with LLMs to dynamically generate and optimize ruin heuristics within the AILS method. Additionally, we introduce an LLM-based acceleration mechanism to enhance computational efficiency. Comprehensive experimental evaluations against state-of-the-art solvers, including AILS-II and HGS, demonstrate the superior performance of AILS-AHD across both moderate and large-scale instances. Notably, our approach establishes new best-known solutions for 8 out of 10 instances in the CVRPLib large-scale benchmark, underscoring the potential of LLM-driven heuristic design in advancing the field of vehicle routing optimization.

A German-context persona stored in `task_iter4_german.txt`. Key differences from the English profile:

title: [2606.27047v1] NuclearQAv2: A Structured Benchmark for Evaluating Domain-Science Competence in Large Language Models
body_excerpt:
## NuclearQAv2: A Structured Benchmark for Evaluating Domain-Science Competence in Large Language Models

**Authors:** Henry Shaowu Yuchi, Michal Kucer, Benjamin H. Sims, Selma Peterson, Emily Taylor
**Published:** 2026-06-25
**Categories:** `cs.CL`, `cs.AI`

**Links:** [abs](http://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27047v1) | [pdf](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.27047v1)

---

### Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance across a wide range of tasks, but ensuring their reliability in highly technical domains remains a significant challenge. In nuclear engineering, problem solving often requires not only factual knowledge but also quantitative reasoning and conceptual understanding. To address the need for systematic evaluation in this domain, we introduce NuclearQAv2, a benchmark for assessing LLMs on nuclear engineering knowledge. The benchmark comprises approximately 1,240 question-answer pairs spanning three categories: boolean, numeric, and verbal. NuclearQAv2 is constructed using a hybrid pipeline that combines expert-authored questions, existing datasets, and LLM-assisted generation from domain-specific technical corpora. By leveraging structured prompting for both automated question generation and response evaluation, the proposed framework enables scalable benchmark construction and evaluation. We evaluate a diverse set of LLMs using NuclearQAv2 and observe substantial performance differences across task types. While the models generally perform well on factual questions, quantitative reasoning and conceptual understanding remain considerably more challenging. These results highlight the importance of multi-faceted evaluation frameworks and establish NuclearQAv2 as a scalable benchmark for assessing LLM capabilities in technical domains.
